improvementsForA: Replace the placeholder rune/glyph rules text on every card with real legible type -- as rendered, no card name, type line, or rules text is readable anywhere on the field, which reads as unfinished despite the polish.

Dial back the global yellow bloom/haze: in field-corner-tl the stream, fence, and flowers are washed to near-blur, and the same amber veil flattens local contrast across the whole field. Keep the golden-hour grade but restore detail contrast in the corners.

The ground texture visibly bleeds over card faces (clearest in field-card-contact and field-hand): parchment areas pick up green grass mottling as if the cards were printed under the field. Mask cards out of the ground texture/grade so paper stays clean and the card reads as a separate physical object.
Differentiate the hand from board cards: the four hand cards lie flat on the grass exactly like fielded cards, with no fan, lift, or scale change, so the hand does not read as held cards.
In field-corner-tr the large tree canopy has semi-translucent yellow facets that read as stained glass rather than sunlit foliage; unify the foliage material with the opaque trees elsewhere.
Tighten the divider's glow falloff -- the seam itself is beautifully integrated, but its bloom smears into adjacent grass and contributes to the overall haze.
improvementsForB: The environment is essentially a graybox: a flat mustard ground plane with visible horizontal banding stripes and zero ground cover between the tree ring and the play area. It needs an actual grass material, flowers/clutter, and painterly value variation before it reads as a meadow at all.

There is no coherent light: nothing on the field casts a shadow (trees, fence, rocks, cards all sit shadowless), so every object floats. Pick a sun direction and add unified cast shadows plus warm/cool grading.

Both water features (top-left and bottom-right corners) read as floating angular UI panels -- hard-edged blue polygons with loose cyan rectangles inside -- rather than ponds with banks that meet the ground. Resolve their shorelines and reflections.
The top-left fence rails hover with no contact shadow and the posts do not visibly meet the ground; ground every prop.
Cards are flat stickers: no edge thickness, near-invisible drop shadows, and deck stacks show no stacked-paper depth. Add card edges and contact-darkened shadows so cards sit on the world.

Palette and art cohesion: teal card sleeves and purple card backs fight the mustard field, and the card art is repeated silhouette screen-print (the same black cat on many cards). The typography and readable rules text are genuinely excellent -- keep that layer and bring the illustration/material quality up to match.
notes: A reads as a painted place: coherent golden-hour light, cast shadows, resolved stream/fence/flower corners, card stacks with real edge thickness, and a divider that crackles through the grass rather than sitting on top of it. B is dramatically more readable as a game (real names, types, and rules text versus A's placeholder glyphs) and its fanned hand is better staged, but its world is an unlit mustard graybox with floating props, panel-like water, and shadowless sticker cards. The decisive factors were environment resolution, light coherence, and card grounding, all of which A wins in nine of ten crops; A's one systemic failure is that nothing on its cards can actually be read.
